stem: A remote pilot stopped drinking 10 hours ago. A breath test now shows an alcohol concentration of 0.04. May the pilot act as remote PIC?

choices.text: No, because 0.04 or greater is prohibited at any time
Yes, because more than 8 hours have passed since the last drink
No, but only because 10 hours is too soon after drinking

explanation.correct: No, because 0.04 or greater is prohibited at any time.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.27 applies 14 CFR 91.17. Section 91.17(a) prohibits acting within 8 hours of drinking, while under the influence, while using a drug that affects one's faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. Each condition stands on its own, so meeting the 8-hour rule does not cure a 0.04 reading. The limit is 0.04 or greater, not above 0.04. The 10 hours since the last drink do satisfy the 8-hour rule; it is the 0.04 concentration that prohibits the flight.
explanation.keyTakeaway: 8 hours AND below 0.04 AND not under the influence. All three must be true.

stem: Official sunset at a job site in Ohio is 5:12 p.m. The pilot's drone has no anti-collision light. What is the latest the drone may be in flight?

choices.text: 5:12 p.m., official sunset
5:42 p.m., the end of evening civil twilight
6:12 p.m., one hour after sunset

explanation.correct: 5:12 p.m., official sunset.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.29(b) and (c) say civil twilight outside Alaska runs from official sunset to 30 minutes after it, and an operation during civil twilight requires anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles. Night follows civil twilight and also requires the lighting under 107.29(a). Without a light, the drone must be on the ground by official sunset. 5:42 p.m. is the end of civil twilight, and the lighting is required throughout that period.
explanation.keyTakeaway: No anti-collision light? Fly only between official sunrise and official sunset.

stem: During a mapping job, the remote PIC places the visual observer behind a parked truck that will block the observer's view of the drone for part of the route. What does Part 107 require?

choices.text: Reposition the observer or change the route so the drone stays in view
Nothing, as long as the remote PIC can see the drone when the observer cannot
Give the observer the drone's video feed to watch instead

explanation.correct: Reposition the observer or change the route so the drone stays in view.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.33(b) requires the remote PIC to ensure that the visual observer is able to see the unmanned aircraft in the manner specified in 107.31, and 107.33(c)(2) requires the crew to maintain awareness of the aircraft's position through direct visual observation. If the observer's view will be blocked, the remote PIC must move the observer or change the route. The remote PIC seeing the drone does not satisfy 107.33(b): when an observer is used, the remote PIC must ensure the observer can see the drone. Watching the drone's video feed does not count; 107.31 requires seeing the aircraft itself with vision unaided by any device other than corrective lenses.
explanation.keyTakeaway: If you use a visual observer, you must make sure the observer can actually see the drone.

stem: A two-drone light show is planned. One crew member would be the remote PIC of drone 1 and, at the same time, the visual observer for drone 2. Without a waiver, this is:

choices.text: Prohibited, because no one may take part in two operations at once
Allowed, because the person is the remote PIC of only one of the two aircraft
Prohibited, because only one drone may fly at a site at a time

explanation.correct: Prohibited, because no one may take part in two operations at once.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.35 says a person may not manipulate flight controls or act as remote PIC or visual observer in the operation of more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time. Mixing the roles across two aircraft is still taking part in two operations at once. The rule can be waived under 107.205(e). Several drones may fly at one site, each with its own crew; what 107.35 prohibits is one person flying or acting as remote PIC or VO for more than one aircraft at the same time.
explanation.keyTakeaway: One person, one aircraft at a time, whether as pilot, controller, or visual observer.

stem: A lab asks a remote pilot to deliver medical samples packed in dry ice across a campus by drone. Under Part 107, this is:

choices.text: Allowed, because dry ice is not flammable or explosive
Prohibited, because dry ice is a hazardous material
Prohibited, because drones may never carry any cargo

explanation.correct: Prohibited, because dry ice is a hazardous material.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.36 prohibits a small unmanned aircraft from carrying hazardous material as defined in 49 CFR 171.8. AIM 11-4-5 lists dry ice, lithium batteries, and aerosol whipped cream as examples of dangerous goods, and says carrying hazardous materials under Part 107 is prohibited and not subject to waiver. Being nonflammable does not make a material non-hazardous. Drones may carry cargo; what 107.36 prohibits is carrying hazardous material.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Dry ice, aerosols, and lithium batteries as cargo are hazmat, and 107.36 cannot be waived.

stem: A low-flying helicopter is approaching the drone's position. The remote PIC thinks the fastest way to avoid it is to pass just underneath it. Under Part 107, the remote PIC must:

choices.text: Hold altitude, because the helicopter pilot must see and avoid the drone
Pass underneath quickly, because staying below manned aircraft is always safe
Give way, and do not pass over, under, or ahead unless well clear

explanation.correct: Give way, and do not pass over, under, or ahead unless well clear.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.37(a) requires a small unmanned aircraft to yield the right of way to all aircraft. Yielding means giving way and not passing over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft unless well clear. Section 107.37(b) also prohibits operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard. The drone never has the right of way over a helicopter.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The drone always yields. Do not pass over, under, or ahead unless well clear.

stem: During a real estate shoot with a drone not eligible for any operations-over-people category, the client's two employees stand in the open yard to watch. The remote PIC wants to fly over them. Are the employees direct participants?

choices.text: No, because only crewmembers count as direct participants
Yes, because they work for the company that hired the pilot
No, because they did not sign a written liability waiver

explanation.correct: No, because only crewmembers count as direct participants.
explanation.reason: No. 14 CFR 107.39(a) permits flight over a person who is directly participating in the operation. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3, says direct participants include the remote PIC, another person manipulating the controls, a visual observer, or crewmembers necessary for the safety of the operation, assigned and briefed by the remote PIC. Working for the client or being told about the flight does not make someone a direct participant. Notice matters only at closed- or restricted-access sites (Category 3, and moving-vehicle operations under 107.145), and this is neither. Part 107 has no liability-waiver mechanism; signing papers does not make anyone a direct participant.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Onlookers, including the client's staff, are not direct participants.

stem: A job site lies inside the lateral boundaries of the Class E surface area designated for a nearby airport. Before flying there, the remote pilot must:

choices.text: Do nothing, because Class E airspace never requires an authorization
Establish two-way radio contact with the airport before launch
Get prior authorization from ATC before the flight

explanation.correct: Get prior authorization from ATC before the flight.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization to operate in Class B, C, or D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport. Most Class E airspace needs no authorization, but a Class E surface area does. Two-way radio contact is a manned-aircraft requirement; Part 107 requires authorization, not radio contact.
explanation.keyTakeaway: B, C, D, and Class E surface areas: prior ATC authorization. Radio contact does not satisfy it.

stem: A remote pilot is filming in Class G airspace a quarter mile from a hospital helipad. A medical helicopter is inbound. Which rule applies?

choices.text: Nothing special, because 107.43 applies only to airports with runways
Avoid interfering with operations at the helipad, as at any airport
Get prior ATC authorization, because the helipad is within a quarter mile

explanation.correct: Avoid interfering with operations at the helipad, as at any airport.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.43 prohibits operating a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10.1, says no notification or authorization is needed near an airport unless the flight is in controlled airspace, but the pilot must avoid traffic patterns and approach paths. In Class G airspace there is no authorization requirement, but the duty not to interfere still applies.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Airports, heliports, and seaplane bases: never interfere with their traffic, even in Class G.

stem: A job lies inside a restricted area. The remote pilot needs to know whom to ask for permission. Where can the pilot find the controlling agency?

choices.text: In the special use airspace table on the sectional chart
In the METAR for the nearest airport, under the remarks section
On the remote pilot's LAANC authorization, which names the agency

explanation.correct: In the special use airspace table on the sectional chart.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.45 requires permission from the using or controlling agency to operate in a restricted area. The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says prohibited, restricted, and warning areas are listed on the sectional chart with their altitude, time of use, and controlling agency or contact facility. A METAR is a weather report, and LAANC grants access to controlled airspace around airports, not permission for a restricted area.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Restricted area? The chart's special use airspace table lists the controlling agency.

stem: A wildfire is burning, and a NOTAM has set up a 14 CFR 91.137(a)(1) temporary flight restriction around it. A certificated remote pilot wants to fly his own drone inside it to send video to the fire crews, without coordinating with anyone. This is:

choices.text: Allowed, because the video would help the emergency response
Prohibited, unless the drone stays below 100 feet AGL
Prohibited, unless the flight is part of the relief effort

explanation.correct: Prohibited, unless the flight is part of the relief effort.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.47 requires remote PICs to comply with 14 CFR 91.137 through 91.145. Under 91.137(b), when a TFR is issued under 91.137(a)(1), no person may operate an aircraft in the area unless it is participating in hazard relief and operating under the direction of the official in charge of on-scene emergency response. Good intentions without that direction do not qualify, and the TFR has no altitude exception for drones.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Disaster TFRs: fly only as part of the response, under the on-scene official's direction.

stem: A fixed-wing drone's telemetry shows a groundspeed of 95 mph. Is this within the Part 107 speed limit?

choices.text: No; the limit is 87 mph
Yes; the limit is 87 knots, which is 100 mph
Yes; Part 107 limits airspeed, not groundspeed

explanation.correct: Yes; the limit is 87 knots, which is 100 mph.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.51(a) limits groundspeed to 87 knots (100 miles per hour). 95 mph is below 100 mph, so it is within the limit. The trap is mixing units: the limit is 87 knots, not 87 mph. 95 mph is about 83 knots, which is less than 87 knots. The limit in 107.51(a) applies to groundspeed, not airspeed.
explanation.keyTakeaway: 87 knots = 100 mph. Check the units on the display.

stem: The METAR for an airport 10 miles away reports 5 statute miles visibility. At the job site, fog limits visibility from the control station to about 2 statute miles. May the pilot fly?

choices.text: Yes, because the nearest official report shows more than 3 statute miles
No, because visibility is judged from the control station
No, because that airport is too far away to use its report

explanation.correct: No, because visibility is judged from the control station.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.51(c) requires a minimum flight visibility of 3 statute miles as observed from the location of the control station. An official report from another location does not override what the pilot actually sees at the site. The airport's distance is not the issue: even a report from next door would not replace the visibility observed from the control station.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Visibility is what you see from the control station: at least 3 statute miles.

stem: A drone at 250 feet AGL is approaching a cloud bank that lies about 1,500 feet ahead at the same altitude. What does Part 107 require?

choices.text: Continue, because the drone is more than 500 feet from the cloud
Turn away, but only once within 500 feet of the cloud
Turn away or stop, to stay 2,000 feet horizontally from it

explanation.correct: Turn away or stop, to stay 2,000 feet horizontally from it.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.51(d) requires the small unmanned aircraft to remain at least 500 feet below a cloud and 2,000 feet horizontally from a cloud. 1,500 feet horizontally is too close. The 500-foot figure is the vertical clearance below a cloud, not the horizontal clearance, and the cloud clearance limits apply at every altitude.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Cloud clearance: 500 feet below, 2,000 feet horizontally.

stem: A pilot passed the initial knowledge test and holds a temporary Remote Pilot Certificate issued two weeks ago. The permanent card has not arrived. May the pilot act as remote PIC?

choices.text: No; only the permanent certificate allows a person to act as remote PIC
Yes, because a temporary certificate is valid for up to 120 days
Only under the direct supervision of another certificated remote pilot

explanation.correct: Yes, because a temporary certificate is valid for up to 120 days.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.12(b) requires a remote PIC to hold a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating and to meet the recency requirement of 107.65. Under 107.64, a temporary certificate is issued for up to 120 calendar days and expires on its expiration date, on receipt of the permanent certificate, or on notice of denial or revocation. A valid temporary certificate meets the requirement, and a pilot who has just passed the initial test also meets recency.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A temporary certificate is a real certificate for up to 120 days.

stem: A pre-programmed mapping route will take the drone behind a hill, out of sight of both the remote PIC and the visual observer, for about two minutes. Under Part 107, this is:

choices.text: Not allowed, because the drone must stay within line of sight
Allowed, because automated flights are exempt from the line-of-sight rule
Not allowed, because automated flight is banned under Part 107

explanation.correct: Not allowed, because the drone must stay within line of sight.
explanation.reason: Automated operation is allowed under Part 107, but the operation must comply with every applicable rule (107.19(d)) and the remote PIC must be able to direct the aircraft (107.19(e)). 14 CFR 107.31 still requires the remote PIC, person at the controls, or a visual observer to see the aircraft throughout the flight. Being able to take control does not replace visual line of sight. Automated flight is allowed under Part 107 as long as the remote PIC can direct the aircraft (AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.2.3); the problem is the loss of visual line of sight.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Automated is fine. Out of sight is not.

stem: Official sunrise in Georgia is 6:45 a.m. A remote pilot launches at 6:20 a.m. What lighting does Part 107 require?

choices.text: None, because the flight begins less than 30 minutes before sunrise
Red and green position lights, the same as manned aircraft at night
Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles

explanation.correct: Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.29(c)(1) defines morning civil twilight outside Alaska as the 30 minutes before official sunrise, here 6:15 to 6:45 a.m. Under 107.29(b), any operation during civil twilight requires lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles. A takeoff at 6:20 a.m. falls in that period. Part 107 requires anti-collision lighting, not position lights.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Civil twilight: 30 minutes before sunrise and 30 minutes after sunset. Both need the 3-statute-mile anti-collision light.

stem: A drone weighs 48 pounds. A customer wants it to carry an 8-pound package to a farm in the same State, within visual line of sight. Can this be done under Part 107?

choices.text: Yes, because the 55-pound limit applies to the aircraft but not its cargo
No, because Part 107 never allows carrying property for hire
No, because the aircraft and package together are over the limit

explanation.correct: No, because the aircraft and package together are over the limit.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.3 defines a small unmanned aircraft as weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything on board or attached. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.15.1, confirms the aircraft plus any property carried must be under 55 pounds. 48 plus 8 is 56 pounds. Staying in one State is required, but it does not fix the weight problem. Part 107 does allow carrying property for compensation or hire within a single State when the total weight stays under 55 pounds and the other conditions are met; the weight is what rules this job out.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Under 55 pounds total at takeoff, cargo included.

stem: A remote pilot installs a transponder on a drone so that ATC radar can see it near a Class C airport. Under Part 107, the drone may be flown with the transponder on:

choices.text: Only if otherwise authorized by the Administrator
Any time it flies in Class C airspace
Only if it flies inside a Class B Mode C veil

explanation.correct: Only if otherwise authorized by the Administrator.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.52 prohibits operating a small UAS with a transponder on unless the Administrator has authorized it otherwise. Being in Class C airspace does not create an exception. Part 107 operations in Class C airspace rely on prior ATC authorization, not a transponder. The Mode C veil does not change the rule; 107.52 allows a transponder to be on only when the Administrator authorizes it.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Transponder on only with FAA authorization, the same as ADS-B Out.

stem: A drone carries a receive-only ADS-B In unit that shows nearby manned traffic on the controller. It has no ADS-B Out equipment. Does 14 CFR 107.53 prohibit this?

choices.text: No; 107.53 prohibits only operating with ADS-B Out transmitting
Yes; all ADS-B equipment, including receivers, is prohibited on small UAS
No, because 107.53 applies only in controlled airspace

explanation.correct: No; 107.53 prohibits only operating with ADS-B Out transmitting.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.53 says no person may operate a small UAS with ADS-B Out equipment in transmit mode unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator. The rule addresses transmitting, not receiving traffic information. A receive-only unit does not transmit, so 107.53 does not apply and no waiver is involved. 107.53 applies in all airspace; it simply does not cover receive-only ADS-B In equipment.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The ban is on transmitting ADS-B Out. Receiving traffic information is not covered.

stem: An applicant was convicted under a State law for possessing marijuana six months ago and now applies for a Remote Pilot Certificate. What may the FAA do?

choices.text: Nothing, because only a Federal drug conviction affects an application
Deny the application for up to 1 year after the conviction
Deny it permanently, because any drug conviction is disqualifying

explanation.correct: Deny the application for up to 1 year after the conviction.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.57(a) says a conviction for violating any Federal or State statute relating to the possession of marijuana, among other drug offenses, is grounds for denying an application for up to 1 year after the date of final conviction, or for suspending or revoking a certificate already held. State convictions count. The denial period is up to 1 year, not permanent.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Federal or State drug convictions: denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation of a held certificate.

stem: After a reported incident, the FAA asks a certificated remote pilot to authorize release of the results of an alcohol test taken at the scene. The pilot refuses. Under Part 107, this refusal is grounds for:

choices.text: Nothing, because only a refusal to a law enforcement officer counts
Suspension or revocation of the Remote Pilot Certificate
A civil penalty only; the certificate cannot be affected

explanation.correct: Suspension or revocation of the Remote Pilot Certificate.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.59 makes it grounds for denial of an application (for up to 1 year) or suspension or revocation of a certificate to refuse a test when a law enforcement officer requests it under 91.17(c), or to refuse to furnish or authorize release of test results that the Administrator requests under 91.17(c) or (d). A refusal to the FAA counts as well as a refusal to an officer. The rule specifically puts the certificate at risk.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Refusing the test, or refusing to release the results to the FAA, can cost you the certificate.

stem: A client tells the remote pilot that the manufacturer says the drone is fine to fly over the crowd at its event. Who is responsible for confirming that the aircraft is eligible for the category of operation being flown?

choices.text: The manufacturer, since it built the aircraft and declared its category
The client, since the client organized the event and invited the crowd
The remote pilot, who must verify the label and DOC listing

explanation.correct: The remote pilot, who must verify the label and DOC listing.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.13, says the remote pilot is responsible for determining that the aircraft is being operated in the appropriate category and for verifying that it is properly labeled and listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance. 14 CFR 107.19 makes the remote PIC the final authority for the operation. The manufacturer's statements and the client's plans do not shift that responsibility.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Over people, the remote pilot owns the eligibility check: category, label, and DOC listing.

stem: A 0.5-pound drone with no exposed rotating parts is used for Category 1 operations. For a night flight over people, the pilot adds a strobe that brings the total weight to 0.6 pounds. Which is correct?

choices.text: The drone still qualifies for Category 1, because anti-collision lights required at night are not counted
The drone no longer qualifies for Category 1, because the 0.55-pound limit includes the light
The drone qualifies for Category 2 automatically, because it is over 0.55 pounds

explanation.correct: The drone no longer qualifies for Category 1, because the 0.55-pound limit includes the light.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.110(a)(1) requires a Category 1 aircraft to weigh 0.55 pounds or less on takeoff and throughout the operation, including everything on board or otherwise attached, and the light is attached. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.14, says the categories and their restrictions do not change at night. Nothing exempts a required light from the weight. Category 2 requires an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance and a label, so it is never automatic.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Night does not change the categories. The light counts toward Category 1's 0.55 pounds.

stem: A remote pilot has a 0.5-pound drone, weighed with everything attached, that has no exposed rotating parts that could cut skin. What else is required before flying it over people under Category 1?

choices.text: Nothing more; Category 1 needs no label or declaration
A Category 1 label in English, applied by the remote pilot
An FAA-accepted declaration of compliance for the model

explanation.correct: Nothing more; Category 1 needs no label or declaration.
explanation.reason: Under 14 CFR 107.110, Category 1 eligibility depends only on weighing 0.55 pounds or less, everything included, and having no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.11.1, says the FAA does not require labeling of Category 1 aircraft. Declarations of compliance apply to Categories 2 and 3. Sustained flight over an open-air assembly still requires Remote ID compliance under 107.110(b).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Category 1: 0.55 pounds or less and no lacerating exposed rotating parts. No DOC and no label.

stem: A remote pilot wants to hover for several minutes over 10 people standing in an open lot. The area is not a closed site and the group is not an open-air assembly. Which category allows this?

choices.text: Category 2
Category 3
Neither; sustained flight over people is never allowed

explanation.correct: Category 2.
explanation.reason: Category 2 under 14 CFR 107.115 places no limit on sustained flight over people, apart from the Remote ID requirement for sustained flight over open-air assemblies. Category 3 under 107.125(c) allows flight over people only within or over a closed- or restricted-access site with everyone on notice or, outside such a site, with no sustained flight over anyone who is neither participating nor under a covered structure or in a stationary vehicle. Hovering over non-participants in an open lot fails both Category 3 conditions.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Category 2 allows sustained flight over people. Category 3 does not, unless at a closed site with everyone on notice.

stem: A drone that is labeled and listed for Category 3 makes one quick pass over a pedestrian on a public sidewalk on its way across a job site. The site is not closed. Is this allowed?

choices.text: No; Category 3 never allows flight over a person outside a closed site
Yes, because a public sidewalk is not part of the job site
Yes, because a single brief pass is not sustained flight

explanation.correct: Yes, because a single brief pass is not sustained flight.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.125(c)(2) allows Category 3 flight above a person if the aircraft does not maintain sustained flight over any person who is not directly participating, under a covered structure, or inside a stationary vehicle. A brief, one-time pass is not sustained flight. The notice requirement in 107.125(c)(1) applies to the other option, a closed- or restricted-access site. Where the pedestrian stands does not matter; the pass is allowed because it is not sustained flight (107.125(c)(2)).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Category 3 outside a closed site: brief passes are allowed; sustained flight over non-participants is not.

stem: A small unmanned aircraft has an airworthiness certificate issued under Part 21, but the operating limitations in its approved Flight Manual prohibit flight over people. May it be used for Category 4 operations?

choices.text: No, because its operating limitations must allow flight over people
Yes, because the airworthiness certificate alone makes it eligible
No, because Category 4 also requires a declaration of compliance

explanation.correct: No, because its operating limitations must allow flight over people.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.140(b) requires a Category 4 aircraft to have an airworthiness certificate under Part 21 and to be operated under the operating limitations in its approved Flight Manual or as specified by the Administrator, and those limitations must not prohibit operations over people. The certificate alone is not enough. Part 107 has no Category 4 label; labeling applies to Categories 2 and 3. Category 4 relies on a Part 21 airworthiness certificate and its operating limitations, not a declaration of compliance (107.140).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Category 4 = Part 21 airworthiness certificate + operating limitations that allow flight over people.

stem: A remote pilot's drone does not qualify for any operations-over-people category. The job is in a busy public park on a Saturday. Which plan follows FAA guidance for selecting the operational area?

choices.text: Fly over park visitors only briefly, so the flight is never sustained
Pick a time and place with no people, or keep them clear
Post a sign announcing the flight, so anyone who reads it is on notice

explanation.correct: Pick a time and place with no people, or keep them clear.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3, says a remote pilot can comply with the rule against flight over people by selecting an operational location where no people are present or expected for the duration, or, if people are present, by having a plan to keep them clear, such as asking them to stay indoors or under safe cover. 14 CFR 107.39 does not allow even brief flight over non-participants for an aircraft that qualifies for no category; the brief-pass allowance belongs to Category 3. Posting notice matters only at closed- or restricted-access sites (Category 3, and moving-vehicle operations under 107.145).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Pick a spot and time with no people, or a plan to keep them clear. Brief flights over them are still flights over them.

stem: What minimum distance from people who are not participating does Part 107 require a remote pilot to keep?

choices.text: None; the remote pilot chooses a safe stand-off distance
500 feet in any direction, the same as for manned aircraft
100 feet horizontally from any person not participating

explanation.correct: None; the remote pilot chooses a safe stand-off distance.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3.1, says Part 107 does not impose a specific stand-off distance from people. The remote pilot may set one by considering the aircraft's performance, environmental conditions such as wind and gusts, the operational area, probable failures and emergency maneuvers, and the pilot's own familiarity with the aircraft, and should adjust it as conditions change. The 500-foot distance comes from the manned-aircraft minimum safe altitude rule in Part 91, which does not apply to Part 107.
explanation.keyTakeaway: No fixed buffer in Part 107. The pilot sets one based on the aircraft, the conditions, and possible failures.

stem: At a closed quarry, haul trucks move constantly. Every driver has been told that a drone may fly over them. Can a Category 2 drone fly sustained flight over the moving trucks?

choices.text: Yes, because everyone in the trucks at the closed site is on notice
No; sustained flight over moving vehicles is never allowed in Category 2
Yes, because haul trucks do not count as vehicles

explanation.correct: Yes, because everyone in the trucks at the closed site is on notice.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.145(b) allows Category 1, 2, or 3 operations over people in moving vehicles if the aircraft either stays within or over a closed- or restricted-access site with everyone in the moving vehicles on notice, or does not maintain sustained flight over moving vehicles. Here the first condition is met, so sustained flight is permitted. The trucks do not need to stop. The haul trucks are moving vehicles under 107.145; the flight is allowed only because the site is closed and the drivers are on notice.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Moving vehicles, Categories 1 to 3: a closed site with everyone on notice, or no sustained flight.

stem: A remote pilot modifies a Category 2-labeled drone in a way its operating instructions do not allow. From now on the pilot will fly it only away from people. What should happen to the Category 2 label?

choices.text: It can stay, because the aircraft will not be flown over people
It should be removed or covered, since it is now ineligible
It can stay until the FAA rescinds the declaration of compliance

explanation.correct: It should be removed or covered, since it is now ineligible.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.4.4, says a modification not permitted by the remote pilot operating instructions renders the aircraft ineligible. FAA guidance in paragraph 8.11.2.4 says that when a modified aircraft is no longer eligible in its labeled category, the person who did the modification would have to remove or cover the old label. Leaving a wrong label invites someone to fly it over people later. The FAA does not need to rescind the declaration for a modified aircraft to become ineligible.
explanation.keyTakeaway: An unapproved modification ends eligibility, and the old label must come off or be covered.

stem: A film crew sets up a Category 3 operation in a fenced lot. Workers who are not part of the drone crew will be inside. What should the remote pilot do about these workers?

choices.text: Nothing, because a fence by itself makes the lot a closed site
Put them on notice of the flights and keep others out
Require each worker to wear a hard hat in place of giving notice

explanation.correct: Put them on notice of the flights and keep others out.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.125(c)(1) allows Category 3 flight over people within a closed- or restricted-access site only if everyone inside is on notice that a drone may fly over them. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3.6.6, says people performing other functions at the site must be on notice and should be advised of precautions, and the remote pilot is responsible for making sure no inadvertent or unauthorized access occurs. A fence helps control access but does not give notice. Protective gear is not a substitute for notice.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Category 3 closed site: control access, and put everyone inside on notice.

stem: A remote pilot buys a used drone that its manufacturer declared eligible for Category 3. Which information must the manufacturer's remote pilot operating instructions cover?

choices.text: The aircraft's maintenance records, flight hours, and repair history
Required components, limits, category, and allowed modifications
The airspace authorizations and waivers the aircraft has received

explanation.correct: Required components, limits, category, and allowed modifications.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.130(b)(2) requires the applicant to make remote pilot operating instructions available on sale or transfer. At a minimum they must cover a system description, including required components, limitations, and declared categories; modifications that do not affect eligibility; and how to verify and change the mode or configuration if it can vary. Maintenance records and airspace authorizations are not part of these instructions.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Operating instructions: components, limits, category, allowed modifications, and mode switching.

stem: The operating instructions for a Category 2 drone list a parachute as a required component for Category 2. The parachute is shipped separately and is not installed today. May the drone be flown over people under Category 2?

choices.text: No, because a required component for Category 2 is missing
Yes, because the Category 2 label is still on the aircraft
No, because parachutes are banned on Category 2 drones

explanation.correct: No, because a required component for Category 2 is missing.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.12.1, says the remote pilot operating instructions must identify any component that must be on the aircraft to meet the Category 2 or 3 safety requirements, including one provided separately such as a parachute. 14 CFR 107.115(a) requires an aircraft that is eligible for Category 2 under 107.120(a). A missing required component means the aircraft is not in its eligible configuration, regardless of the label. Parachutes are not banned; here the operating instructions make one a required component.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Required components are part of eligibility. If one is missing, the aircraft is not eligible.

stem: A Category 2 drone's operating instructions list two approved replacement cameras as optional components. The pilot swaps in one of the listed cameras and secures it. Is the drone still eligible for Category 2?

choices.text: Yes, because the camera is listed and securely attached
No; any change at all requires a new declaration of compliance
Yes, and any other payload may now be added without affecting eligibility

explanation.correct: Yes, because the camera is listed and securely attached.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.12.1, item 2a, says the operating instructions must completely describe modifications that do not change eligibility, including any payload, consistent with 14 CFR 107.120(b)(2)(ii). The sample instructions in Figure 8-2 allow replacing the camera only with a pre-approved camera listed in the instructions, and require any permissible payload to be securely attached. A listed camera, securely attached, keeps eligibility; an unlisted payload may end it. Not every change requires a new declaration.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Listed optional components keep eligibility. Unlisted payloads may end it.

stem: A hobbyist builds a drone from parts bought separately, not from a kit, and wants to fly it over people under Category 3. What must happen first?

choices.text: Nothing, because drones built by a hobbyist are exempt from Subpart D
The builder only needs to put a Category 3 label on the aircraft
The builder must use an accepted MOC and submit a DOC

explanation.correct: The builder must use an accepted MOC and submit a DOC.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.4.2, says someone who builds a small unmanned aircraft from separate parts, not from a kit, is an applicant and must submit a declaration of compliance to conduct Category 2 or 3 operations. Under 14 CFR 107.160, the declaration identifies the FAA-accepted means of compliance used to show the aircraft meets 107.130(a). Home-built aircraft get no exemption from Subpart D, and a label without an accepted declaration does not make an aircraft eligible.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Building it yourself makes you the applicant: accepted MOC first, then a DOC.

stem: A client wants a remote pilot to file a declaration of compliance so that the client's unmodified, store-bought drone can be flown over people under Category 2. What is a declaration of compliance, and who submits it?

choices.text: A record of Category 2 or 3 compliance from the producer, designer, or modifier
A form the remote pilot submits to the FAA before each operation over people
An FAA report issued after the aircraft passes a test flight with an inspector

explanation.correct: A record of Category 2 or 3 compliance from the producer, designer, or modifier.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.3 defines a declaration of compliance as a record submitted to the FAA that certifies the small unmanned aircraft conforms to the Category 2 or Category 3 requirements of Subpart D. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.9, says it is submitted by the person who designs, produces, or modifies the aircraft. For an unmodified aircraft, the remote pilot's job is to verify that the model is listed on an FAA-accepted declaration and labeled. It is not filed per operation, and it is not an FAA test flight report.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The DOC comes from whoever produces, designs, or modifies the aircraft. The pilot checks that it is listed.

stem: The operating instructions for a Category 2 drone list a specific propeller as an allowed replacement. During routine maintenance the operator installs that propeller. What is required?

choices.text: A new declaration of compliance, as for any propeller change
Nothing more, because the propeller is an allowed replacement
An FAA airworthiness inspection before the next flight over people

explanation.correct: Nothing more, because the propeller is an allowed replacement.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.4.5, says maintenance on an eligible Category 2 or 3 aircraft that does not change its configuration or characteristics does not require a new declaration of compliance. It gives the example of replacing propellers when that is listed as an allowed modification. Replacing them with propellers not covered by the operating instructions would require a new declaration. Category 2 aircraft have no airworthiness inspection requirement.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Maintenance within the operating instructions keeps eligibility. Unlisted parts need a new DOC.

stem: Under Part 107, how must a means of compliance show that an aircraft meets the Category 2 injury limit?

choices.text: Through a log of flight hours showing the aircraft has never had an accident
Through test, analysis, or inspection that the FAA accepts
Through a demonstration flight observed by the remote pilot's client

explanation.correct: Through test, analysis, or inspection that the FAA accepts.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.155(a) says a means of compliance for Category 2 or 3 must consist of test, analysis, or inspection. Under 107.155(c), the FAA notifies the applicant when it accepts the means of compliance, and AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.5.1, says the FAA must accept it before an applicant can rely on it. Accident-free hours and client demonstrations are not recognized methods.
explanation.keyTakeaway: MOC = test, analysis, or inspection, and the FAA must accept it.

stem: Using the FAA-provided means of compliance, a manufacturer calculates that a drone's maximum impact kinetic energy is 24.8 foot-pounds. For which categories is the drone eligible on that basis?

choices.text: Category 3 only
Category 2 only
Both Category 2 and Category 3

explanation.correct: Category 3 only.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.120(a)(1) limits Category 2 to injury less severe than a transfer of 11 foot-pounds of kinetic energy, and 107.130(a)(1) limits Category 3 to less than 25 foot-pounds. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.6.1.5, gives this example: a 1-pound aircraft with a maximum impact speed of 40 feet per second has about 24.8 foot-pounds. That exceeds the Category 2 limit but is below the Category 3 limit. Eligibility also requires meeting the other requirements and being listed on an accepted declaration.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Under 11 ft-lb: Category 2. Under 25 ft-lb: Category 3.

stem: A ducted-fan drone design keeps its propellers inside a shroud. Tests show the shroud is likely to break in a typical impact with a person and expose the spinning blades. Does it meet the exposed rotating parts requirement?

choices.text: Yes, because the propellers are enclosed during normal flight
No, because every ducted-fan design is automatically ineligible
No, because a typical impact could expose the blades

explanation.correct: No, because a typical impact could expose the blades.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.6.2, says propellers internal to the aircraft, as in a ducted fan, satisfy the requirement only if they would not contact a person in a typical impact. If impact forces are likely to cause structural failures that expose the rotating parts, the design does not satisfy it. The requirement applies to Categories 1, 2, and 3 under 14 CFR 107.110(a)(2), 107.120(a)(2), and 107.130(a)(2). Ducted designs are not automatically ineligible; a shroud that stays intact in typical impacts could meet the requirement.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A shroud counts only if it stays intact in a typical impact with a person.

stem: A university lab wants to test a prototype unmanned aircraft that has no Remote ID equipment, outside any FAA-recognized identification area. Under Part 89, when may it fly without Remote ID?

choices.text: Whenever it flies for a university, because schools are exempt
When it stays below 200 feet AGL on its own campus
When the FAA authorizes it for aeronautical research

explanation.correct: When the FAA authorizes it for aeronautical research.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 89.105 requires Remote ID except as otherwise authorized or as provided in 89.120. Section 89.120 says the Administrator may authorize operations without Remote ID when the operation is solely for aeronautical research or to show compliance with regulations. The other path, 89.115(b), applies only inside an FAA-recognized identification area, which this flight is not. There is no automatic exemption for schools or prototypes. No altitude or campus exception exists; without Remote ID equipment and outside a FRIA, it needs FAA authorization under 89.120.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Outside a FRIA, flying without Remote ID for research needs FAA authorization under 89.120.

stem: A pilot from Canada brings a Canadian-registered drone with Remote ID to the United States for a job. What does Part 89 require before the flight?

choices.text: Submit a notice of identification and carry the confirmation
Nothing, because foreign-registered drones are exempt from Part 89
Re-register the drone with the FAA as a U.S. aircraft before flying

explanation.correct: Submit a notice of identification and carry the confirmation.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 89.130(a) requires anyone operating a foreign-registered civil unmanned aircraft with Remote ID in the United States to submit a notice of identification first. Under 89.130(b) and (c), the FAA issues a Confirmation of Identification, which must be kept at the control station and shown on request to the FAA or a law enforcement officer. Section 89.130(b)(2) says the notice and the confirmation do not count as U.S. aircraft registration.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Foreign-registered drones with Remote ID: notice of identification, then keep the Confirmation of Identification at the control station.

stem: A Part 107 pilot says his drone does not need Remote ID because Part 89 exempts unmanned aircraft that transmit ADS-B Out. Is he right?

choices.text: No; that exemption covers only Part 91 ADS-B Out operations
Yes; any unmanned aircraft transmitting ADS-B Out is exempt from Remote ID
No; Part 89 has no exceptions to Remote ID of any kind

explanation.correct: No; that exemption covers only Part 91 ADS-B Out operations.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 89.101(b) says the Remote ID operating rules do not apply to unmanned aircraft operations under Part 91 that are transmitting ADS-B Out under 91.225. A Part 107 operation is not a Part 91 operation. Section 89.125 says ADS-B Out cannot be used to comply with Remote ID, and 14 CFR 107.53 prohibits a Part 107 operation from transmitting ADS-B Out unless authorized. Part 89 does have an exception, in 89.101(b), but it is limited to operations under Part 91 that transmit ADS-B Out under 91.225.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part 107 drones: ADS-B Out is not Remote ID, and transmitting it is banned without authorization.

stem: A standard Remote ID unmanned aircraft must broadcast its identity. Part 89 allows that identity to be either its serial number or:

choices.text: Its session ID for the flight
Its pilot's certificate number
Its registration number

explanation.correct: Its session ID for the flight.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 89.305(a) says a standard Remote ID unmanned aircraft must broadcast the identity of the aircraft, consisting of either a serial number assigned by the producer or a session ID. The pilot's certificate number and the registration number are not message elements under 89.305.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Standard Remote ID identity: serial number or session ID.

stem: A remote pilot buys a Remote ID broadcast module to add to an older drone. How can the pilot tell the module was produced to meet Part 89?

choices.text: It carries a permanent English label saying it meets Part 89
Its packaging says it is compatible with the pilot's drone model
It transmits on the same 2.4 GHz band as the drone's controller

explanation.correct: It carries a permanent English label saying it meets Part 89.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 89.525(b) says no one may produce a Remote ID broadcast module unless it displays a label indicating it meets Part 89, in English and legible, prominent, and permanently affixed. Under 89.115(a)(1)(i), its serial number must also be listed on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance. Compatibility claims and radio frequency do not show compliance.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Compliant modules carry a permanent Part 89 label, and their serial numbers are on an accepted DOC.

stem: A remote pilot's controller fails during preflight, and the aircraft itself is undamaged. Under the Part 107 definition, is the small UAS in a condition for safe operation?

choices.text: No, because the controller is part of the small UAS
Yes, because the small UAS means only the aircraft itself
No, because a mechanic must inspect the aircraft first

explanation.correct: No, because the controller is part of the small UAS.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.3 defines a small unmanned aircraft system as the small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements, including communication links and the components that control it, that are required for safe and efficient operation. The control station is part of the system, so a failed controller means the system is not in a condition for safe operation under 107.15. The remote PIC must also be able to direct the aircraft under 107.19(e). Part 107 does not require a mechanic's inspection; the problem is that the controller is part of the small UAS (107.3).
explanation.keyTakeaway: The 'system' in small UAS includes the control station and the links, not just the aircraft.

stem: A remote pilot sells a registered drone to another company. Under Part 48, what must the seller do?

choices.text: Nothing; the registration transfers automatically to the buyer
Update the registration information within 14 calendar days of the sale
Remove the registration number from the aircraft and keep the certificate until it expires

explanation.correct: Update the registration information within 14 calendar days of the sale.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 48.115(b)(2) requires the holder of a Certificate of Aircraft Registration to update the information in the web-based registration system within 14 calendar days when the registration must be cancelled for any reason, including sale or transfer. Registration does not pass to a buyer automatically; under 48.25(b), the owner must register in the owner's own legal name. Keeping the certificate until it expires does not meet the update requirement.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Sold, destroyed, or exported? Update the registration within 14 calendar days.

stem: A small business owns three drones that it flies under Part 107. How must they be registered?

choices.text: One registration covers all three, as it does for recreational flyers
Only the largest drone, since the others weigh under 2 pounds
Each one must be registered on its own certificate

explanation.correct: Each one must be registered on its own certificate.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 48.100(a) says a Certificate of Aircraft Registration for a small unmanned aircraft used for any purpose other than limited recreational operations constitutes registration for the aircraft identified on the application, and 48.30(a) sets the fee at $5 per aircraft. The single registration covering all of an owner's aircraft applies only to aircraft flown exclusively for recreation under 48.105. Every aircraft flown under Part 107 must be registered.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part 107: one registration per aircraft. Recreational: one registration per owner.

stem: A drone is losing power and must land within seconds. The remote PIC can reach either a crowded restaurant patio or an empty lawn slightly farther away. According to FAA guidance on in-flight emergencies, what should guide the choice?

choices.text: Landing as close as possible, even if that is over the patio
Taking the fastest action, even if it means the patio
Taking the action that minimizes injury and damage, here the empty lawn

explanation.correct: Taking the action that minimizes injury and damage, here the empty lawn.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.21(a) lets the remote PIC deviate from Part 107 to the extent necessary to meet an in-flight emergency. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.18, adds that emergency action should be taken in such a way as to minimize injury or damage to property, and 107.19(c) requires the remote PIC to ensure the aircraft poses no undue hazard to people in a loss of control. The nearest spot is not automatically right if it puts people at risk. Speed is not the test; AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.18, says emergency action should minimize injury or damage to property.
explanation.keyTakeaway: In an emergency, deviate only as needed, and choose the option that keeps people and property safest.

stem: Which situation is an in-flight emergency under Part 107?

choices.text: A client asks for the flight to be finished faster than planned
A motor fails over a road and the drone must land immediately
A battery the pilot knew before takeoff would not last the job

explanation.correct: A motor fails over a road and the drone must land immediately.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.18, describes an in-flight emergency as an unexpected and unforeseen serious occurrence or situation that requires urgent, prompt action, and 14 CFR 107.21(a) allows deviation only for an emergency requiring immediate action. Schedule pressure from a client is not an emergency. A battery problem known before takeoff was foreseen and should have been handled in preflight under 107.49(d), which requires enough power for the intended operational time.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Emergency = unexpected, serious, and needing immediate action. Foreseeable problems belong in preflight.

stem: A pilot wants to fly low and fast alongside moving cars on a busy highway to film a 'chase' scene, passing within a few feet of the vehicles. The drone stays in sight and below 400 feet AGL. This could violate Part 107 because:

choices.text: Part 107 bans all flight within 500 feet of any vehicle on a road
It could be careless or reckless operation endangering others
Highways are restricted areas under 107.45 that require permission

explanation.correct: It could be careless or reckless operation endangering others.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.23(a) prohibits operating a small UAS in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger the life or property of another. Flying within a few feet of moving traffic puts drivers and vehicles at risk even when the altitude and line-of-sight limits are met. Part 107 has no 500-foot vehicle buffer, and a highway is not a restricted area under 107.45. Flying over moving vehicles is also limited by 107.145.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Endangering people or property can be careless or reckless, even within every numeric limit.

stem: An operator asks the FAA for a waiver so that it can perform an operation that would otherwise be careless or reckless. Can 14 CFR 107.23 be waived?

choices.text: Yes, like every section of Part 107 except the airspace rules
No; 107.23 is not on the list of rules that can be waived
No; only Part 107's airspace rules can ever be waived

explanation.correct: No; 107.23 is not on the list of rules that can be waived.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.205 lists the Part 107 sections a certificate of waiver can cover: 107.25, 107.29(a)(2) and (b), 107.31, 107.33, 107.35, 107.37(a), 107.39, 107.41, 107.51, and 107.145. Section 107.23, hazardous operation, is not on the list, so it cannot be waived. An airspace authorization under 107.41 has nothing to do with 107.23. Many non-airspace sections can be waived under 107.205, such as 107.31 and 107.39; 107.23 is simply not among them.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Careless or reckless operation cannot be waived.

stem: A film crew wants to fly a drone from a helicopter that is moving over open, empty desert. Under Part 107 this is:

choices.text: Prohibited, because no one may fly a drone from a moving aircraft
Allowed, because the area is sparsely populated
Prohibited, because helicopters may never carry drones aboard

explanation.correct: Prohibited, because no one may fly a drone from a moving aircraft.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.25(a) prohibits operating a small UAS from a moving aircraft. The sparsely populated exception in 107.25(b) applies only to moving land or water-borne vehicles, not to aircraft. Section 107.25 is waivable under 107.205(a), but there is no exception without a waiver. Carrying a drone aboard is not the problem; operating it from the moving aircraft is (107.25(a)).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Moving car or boat: possible over sparsely populated areas. Moving aircraft: never without a waiver.

stem: A delivery company wants to launch drones carrying packages for paying customers from a moving van in a rural area. Can it get a waiver to do this?

choices.text: Yes; 107.25 can be waived for any purpose, including deliveries
No waiver is needed, because the area is sparsely populated
No; that use of a moving vehicle cannot be waived

explanation.correct: No; that use of a moving vehicle cannot be waived.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.25(b) prohibits operating from a moving land or water-borne vehicle when the aircraft is transporting another person's property for compensation or hire. Section 107.205(a) allows a waiver of 107.25 but states that no waiver will be issued to allow carriage of the property of another for compensation or hire. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.15.1, repeats that this limitation cannot be waived. The sparsely populated exception does not cover carrying property for hire.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Paid deliveries from a moving vehicle: prohibited, and no waiver is available.

stem: The visual observer for a job had a beer with lunch two hours ago. The remote PIC has not had any alcohol. May the observer take part in the flight?

choices.text: Yes, because the alcohol rules apply only to the remote PIC
No; the 8-hour rule applies to visual observers too
No; observers must avoid alcohol for 24 hours before a flight

explanation.correct: No; the 8-hour rule applies to visual observers too.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.27 applies 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19 to the person manipulating the controls, the remote PIC, and the visual observer. Section 91.17(a)(1) prohibits acting within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol. Being under 0.04 does not cure a drink within 8 hours, because each condition in 91.17(a) stands on its own. The rule is 8 hours, the same as for the remote PIC, not 24.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The alcohol rules cover the remote PIC, the person at the controls, and the visual observer.

stem: A person asks a remote pilot to fly a package of marijuana across town by drone. No Federal or State authorization covers the carriage. Under Part 107, this is:

choices.text: Prohibited, because 91.19 bans knowingly carrying such drugs
Allowed where State law permits recreational marijuana use
Prohibited, because Part 107 bans every medication too

explanation.correct: Prohibited, because 91.19 bans knowingly carrying such drugs.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.27 requires the remote PIC, the person at the controls, and the visual observer to comply with 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19. Section 91.19(a) prohibits operating a civil aircraft with knowledge that narcotic drugs, marihuana, or depressant or stimulant drugs are carried in it, unless the carriage is authorized by or under a Federal or State statute or by a Federal or State agency (91.19(b)); a State law simply permitting use is not an authorization to carry the drug by aircraft. Section 107.57(b) makes an act prohibited by 91.19(a) grounds for denial, suspension, or revocation of a Remote Pilot Certificate. Part 107 does not ban every medication; the issue here is carrying marijuana, which 91.19 prohibits.
explanation.keyTakeaway: 107.27 brings in 91.19: knowingly carrying drugs by drone is prohibited unless specifically authorized.

stem: Does Part 107 require a drone to show anti-collision lighting during a midday flight?

choices.text: No; lighting is required only at twilight and night
Yes; anti-collision lighting is required on every flight
No, unless the drone climbs above 200 feet AGL

explanation.correct: No; lighting is required only at twilight and night.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.29 requires anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles only at night and during civil twilight. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.7.2.2, says 107.29 does not require lighting during the day, notes that lighting is generally not effective for daytime collision avoidance, and says pilots may still choose to use it. Altitude does not trigger the lighting rule; only civil twilight and night do (107.29).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Daytime: no lighting required. Civil twilight and night: a 3-statute-mile anti-collision light.

stem: A remote pilot needs to know exactly when a daytime-only flight must end. According to AC 107-2A, where can official sunrise and sunset times be found?

choices.text: The Air Almanac tables, available from the Naval Observatory
The drone manufacturer's app, which sets the legal times
The sectional chart's margin notes for the area

explanation.correct: The Air Almanac tables, available from the Naval Observatory.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.7, says civil twilight and night are defined using The Air Almanac, which provides tables to determine sunrise and sunset at various latitudes, and that these tables can be downloaded from the Naval Observatory. A manufacturer's app may show times, but it does not set legal times. Sectional charts do not list sunrise and sunset.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Official sunrise and sunset come from The Air Almanac.

stem: During a survey, a drone passes behind a tree for a few seconds and the remote PIC loses sight of it. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Sight must be regained as soon as practicable; no set time is allowed
Any loss of sight, however brief, is a violation that must be reported
Losing sight is allowed for up to 30 seconds at a time

explanation.correct: Sight must be regained as soon as practicable; no set time is allowed.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9, says the person keeping visual line of sight may have brief moments without seeing the aircraft, but must regain it as soon as practicable if it is lost, and that no specific time interval is permitted, because a fixed interval could allow a hazardous interruption. If VLOS cannot be regained, the pilot should follow predetermined lost-VLOS procedures. Part 107 has no reporting requirement for a brief loss of sight.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Brief losses happen. Regain sight as soon as practicable. There is no allowed number of seconds.

stem: A drone is far enough away that the remote PIC can see it only as a tiny dot and cannot tell which way it is pointed or moving. Is the operation within visual line of sight?

choices.text: No; the pilot must be able to tell its attitude and direction
Yes, because the drone is still visible as a dot in the sky
No; the drone must always stay within 1,000 feet of the pilot

explanation.correct: No; the pilot must be able to tell its attitude and direction.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.31(a) requires seeing the aircraft throughout the flight in order to know its location, determine its attitude, altitude, and direction of flight, observe the airspace for other traffic or hazards, and determine that it does not endanger anyone. Merely detecting a dot does not meet that standard. Part 107 sets no fixed VLOS distance; the test is whether the pilot can see the aircraft's location, attitude, altitude, and direction (107.31).
explanation.keyTakeaway: VLOS means seeing enough to tell location, attitude, altitude, and direction, not just a dot.

stem: A remote PIC flying alone glances down at the controller for a moment to check the remaining battery. Does this break the visual line of sight requirement?

choices.text: Yes; the pilot must watch the aircraft without any interruption
No; brief looks at the controller are allowed by the FAA
No, as long as the look lasts under 30 seconds

explanation.correct: No; brief looks at the controller are allowed by the FAA.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9, says the person maintaining visual line of sight may have brief moments of not looking directly at the aircraft, for example to check battery life on the controller, while keeping the capability to see it, and that the VLOS requirement does not prohibit briefly looking down at the control station. A visual observer is optional and is not required for such glances. The FAA sets no time allowance: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9, says no specific interval of lost VLOS is permissible, while brief looks at the control station are fine.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A quick look at the controller is fine. Keep the ability to see the aircraft.

stem: During a mapping flight with a visual observer, the remote PIC asks the observer to also run the camera and watch the camera screen continuously. What is the problem?

choices.text: There is no problem, because the camera feed shows the aircraft
The observer must use binoculars to see it directly
The observer must watch the drone directly, not on a screen

explanation.correct: The observer must watch the drone directly, not on a screen.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.33(c) requires the remote PIC, the person at the controls, and the visual observer to coordinate to scan the airspace for potential collision hazards and to maintain awareness of the aircraft's position through direct visual observation. An observer watching a camera screen cannot do either. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9.1, says first-person view does not satisfy visual line of sight. Binoculars may be used only momentarily (AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9.1); the observer must normally see the drone with unaided vision.
explanation.keyTakeaway: An observer's job is direct watching and scanning. Do not load them with screen work.

stem: A remote pilot is flying a simple roof inspection alone, keeping the drone in sight the whole time. Is a visual observer required?

choices.text: No; a visual observer is optional under Part 107
Yes; every Part 107 flight requires a visual observer
No, unless the flight lasts over 15 minutes

explanation.correct: No; a visual observer is optional under Part 107.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9.2, says the use of a visual observer is optional. 14 CFR 107.31(b) allows visual line of sight to be kept by the remote PIC and the person at the controls, or by a visual observer, and 107.33 sets requirements only 'if a visual observer is used.' Flight length does not matter; 107.33 makes a visual observer optional.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A visual observer is optional. If you use one, 107.33 applies.

stem: A helicopter is flying toward the area where a small drone is hovering. The remote PIC assumes the helicopter pilot has seen the drone and will avoid it. What is wrong with this assumption?

choices.text: Nothing, because helicopter pilots must always see and avoid drones
Helicopters cannot see anything below 500 feet AGL
Small drones are hard to see, and the drone must yield anyway

explanation.correct: Small drones are hard to see, and the drone must yield anyway.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-6 warns manned pilots that, because unmanned aircraft can be very small, they may be difficult to see and track. A remote PIC cannot count on being seen. Under 14 CFR 107.37(a), the drone must yield the right of way to all aircraft in any case, and 107.31 gives the remote PIC the see-and-avoid duty. There is no such blind altitude; the point is that small drones are hard to see at any height.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Assume you have not been seen. The drone yields.

stem: A paraglider is soaring along the ridge where a drone is mapping. Who must give way?

choices.text: The paraglider, because the drone was working there first
Neither, because a paraglider is not an aircraft under Part 107
The drone, which must yield to all aircraft and airborne vehicles

explanation.correct: The drone, which must yield to all aircraft and airborne vehicles.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.37(a) requires each small unmanned aircraft to yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles, giving way and not passing over, under, or ahead unless well clear. The rule covers airborne vehicles, so it applies whether or not the paraglider is classed as an aircraft. Who arrived first does not matter.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Drones yield to everything that flies: aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles.

stem: It is a clear, calm day with unlimited visibility, and the remote PIC relaxes the scan for traffic. According to the AIM, when have midair collisions almost always happened?

choices.text: In low visibility and rain
In ideal weather conditions
At night, in darkness

explanation.correct: In ideal weather conditions.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-1 says air collisions have almost invariably occurred under ideal weather conditions, and that unlimited visibility encourages a sense of security that is not justified. It urges pilots to be alert at all times, especially when the weather is good. A remote PIC's see-and-avoid duty under 14 CFR 107.31 and 107.37 does not ease on clear days.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Good weather is when collisions happen. Keep scanning.

stem: A remote pilot wants to fly at 50 feet AGL inside a Class C surface area for a quick roof photo. Does the low altitude remove the need for authorization?

choices.text: No; drones under 100 feet AGL are exempt from 107.41
No, but only because a roof photo counts as commercial work
No; any altitude inside the Class C surface area needs authorization

explanation.correct: No; any altitude inside the Class C surface area needs authorization.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 prohibits operating in Class B, C, or D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport, without prior authorization from ATC. A Class C surface area extends from the surface, so a flight at 50 feet AGL is in Class C. No altitude, such as 100 feet AGL, is exempt. Commercial purpose has nothing to do with it; any flight inside the Class C surface area needs authorization.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Inside B, C, D, or a Class E surface area, any altitude needs prior authorization.

stem: A small non-towered airport is surrounded by a dashed magenta line, and the area around it has Class E airspace beginning at 1,200 feet AGL. A job site is half a mile outside the dashed magenta line. The drone will stay at or below 400 feet AGL. Is ATC authorization required?

choices.text: Yes; anything within a few miles of a dashed magenta line needs authorization
No, as long as the pilot stays in radio contact with ATC
No; the site is outside the Class E surface area and below 1,200 feet AGL

explanation.correct: No; the site is outside the Class E surface area and below 1,200 feet AGL.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says a Class E surface area is shown with a dashed magenta line. 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior authorization only within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport (and in Class B, C, and D airspace). Outside the dashed line, Class E begins here at 1,200 feet AGL, so a drone at or below 400 feet AGL is in Class G and needs no authorization. The boundary is the dashed line itself, not a buffer around it. No radio contact is involved; Part 107 requires prior authorization only in the airspace listed in 107.41, and never requires radio contact.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Inside the dashed magenta line: authorization. Outside it, below the Class E floor: Class G.

stem: A remote pilot's ATC authorization in Class D airspace allows flight up to 200 feet AGL. To get a better angle, the pilot wants to climb to 300 feet AGL. What is correct?

choices.text: The pilot may climb to 400 feet AGL, the Part 107 limit
The pilot may climb if no manned aircraft are in sight
The pilot must stay at or below the authorized altitude

explanation.correct: The pilot must stay at or below the authorized altitude.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization for operation in Class D airspace, and AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10, says authorizations may depend on operational parameters set by ATC. Flying above the authorized altitude means operating in Class D airspace without authorization for that operation. The 400-foot limit in 107.51(b) is a separate maximum and does not expand an authorization.
explanation.keyTakeaway: An authorization's altitude is a limit. Exceeding it is flying without authorization.

stem: A remote pilot arrives at a site and realizes it lies inside Class D airspace. The pilot plans to launch and request authorization once airborne. Is that allowed?

choices.text: Yes, if the pilot requests it within 5 minutes of launch
No; it must be obtained before entering the airspace
No; requests must be submitted at least 90 days ahead

explanation.correct: No; it must be obtained before entering the airspace.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior authorization from ATC to operate in Class B, C, or D airspace or a Class E surface area. 'Prior' means before operating there. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10, says the FAA may approve or deny requests based on traffic, workload, and other factors, so approval cannot be assumed. No grace period makes an unauthorized flight legal. There is no 90-day advance requirement: AIM 11-4-2 says LAANC gives remote pilots near real-time airspace authorization within UAS Facility Map altitudes. What matters is that approval comes before the drone enters the airspace.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Authorization first, then launch.

stem: The Chart Supplement says an airport's Class D airspace becomes a Class E surface area when the tower closes at night. A remote pilot plans to fly there after the tower closes. Is authorization still required?

choices.text: No; authorization is needed only while the tower is open
Yes; Class E surface areas also need authorization
Yes, but only within 1 mile of the runway

explanation.correct: Yes; Class E surface areas also need authorization.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 covers Class B, C, and D airspace and the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport. If the airspace becomes a Class E surface area when the tower closes, the authorization requirement still applies. Whether the tower is open does not decide the matter; the airspace class does. The requirement covers the whole lateral boundary of the Class E surface area, not just the area near the runway.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Tower closed and the airspace becomes a Class E surface area? Still get authorization.

stem: In Class G airspace, a survey site lies under the final approach path a mile from the end of a non-towered airport's runway. What does FAA guidance tell the remote pilot to do?

choices.text: Avoid the corridor so manned pilots never have to change course
Fly normally, because airport rules apply only inside the airport fence
Avoid the corridor only while an airplane is in sight

explanation.correct: Avoid the corridor so manned pilots never have to change course.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraphs 5.10.1 and 5.10.1.2, say the remote PIC must avoid traffic patterns and approach corridors to runways and landing areas, and should operate so that a manned pilot does not need to alter the flight path in the pattern or on an approach. 14 CFR 107.43 prohibits interfering with operations and traffic patterns at any airport. Approach paths extend beyond the airport boundary, and aircraft on final can be well below 400 feet AGL. The guidance is to avoid approach corridors altogether, not only when traffic is visible.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Stay out of approach corridors. Manned pilots should never have to change course for you.

stem: A drone is working near a taxiway at an airport, and an airplane begins to taxi toward the area. Who has the right of way?

choices.text: The drone, because the airplane is not flying yet
The airplane, even though it is on the ground
Neither, because right-of-way rules apply only in the air

explanation.correct: The airplane, even though it is on the ground.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10.1, says that near an airport the remote PIC must yield the right of way to all other aircraft, including aircraft operating on the surface of the airport, and must avoid areas such as taxiways and runways where the drone could interfere (14 CFR 107.43). A taxiing airplane is still an aircraft.
explanation.keyTakeaway: On the ground or in the air, manned aircraft have the right of way.

stem: A remote pilot with an authorization is watching manned traffic in a towered airport's pattern. A helicopter appears from a direction outside the normal pattern. What does the AIM say about helicopters at towered airports?

choices.text: Helicopters must always fly the same left-hand pattern as airplanes
Helicopters are not allowed at airports with a control tower
Helicopters avoid the flow of fixed-wing traffic

explanation.correct: Helicopters avoid the flow of fixed-wing traffic.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-3-2 says that, unless otherwise authorized or directed, fixed-wing aircraft approaching to land must circle the airport to the left, while pilots approaching to land in a helicopter must avoid the flow of fixed-wing traffic. So a remote pilot should expect helicopters outside the airplane pattern and keep scanning in every direction.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Helicopters avoid the airplane pattern. Watch every direction near an airport.

stem: A sectional chart lists a restricted area as active during set times on weekdays. No NOTAM about it has been issued today. Can the remote pilot assume it is inactive?

choices.text: Yes; restricted areas are active only when a NOTAM says so
No; the charted times apply even without a NOTAM
No, because restricted areas are active at all times

explanation.correct: No; the charted times apply even without a NOTAM.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says special use airspace is listed with its altitude, time of use, and controlling agency, and warns that a NOTAM addressing activation will not be issued to announce permanently listed times of use. 14 CFR 107.45 requires permission from the using or controlling agency to operate in a restricted area. Restricted areas are not always active; their charted times of use are what apply.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Charted hours apply without a NOTAM. Check the listed times and get permission.

stem: A NOTAM designates an area around a coastal rocket launch site under 14 CFR 91.143 for a space launch. A remote pilot wants to film the launch from inside the area. Under Part 107:
